bibl.title: Spontaneous behaviors drive multidimensional, brainwide activity

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the structure of spontaneous and stimulus-evoked population activity in mouse visual cortex, and what the apparently noisy component of it encodes
span.quote: Neuronal populations in sensory cortex produce variable responses to sensory stimuli, and exhibit intricate spontaneous activity even without external sensory input.

span.label: is cortical variability random noise, recapitulation of prior sensory experience, or encoding of ongoing behaviour
span.quote: Cortical variability and spontaneous activity have been variously proposed to represent random noise, recall of prior experience, or encoding of ongoing behavioral and cognitive variables.

span.label: shows spontaneous activity reliably encodes a high-dimensional behavioural signal present brain-wide, and that sensory input adds to it in orthogonal dimensions rather than displacing it
span.quote: Thus, visual cortical population activity, despite its apparently noisy structure, reliably encodes an orthogonal fusion of sensory and multidimensional behavioral information.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Recording over 10,000 neurons in mouse visual cortex, we observed that spontaneous activity reliably encoded a high-dimensional latent state, which was partially related to the mouse’s ongoing behavior and was represented not just in visual cortex but across the forebrain.

span.label: spontaneous cortical population activity and trial-to-trial response variability
span.quote: Neuronal populations in sensory cortex produce variable responses to sensory stimuli, and exhibit intricate spontaneous activity even without external sensory input.

span.label: in-vivo-two-photon-calcium-imaging
span.quote: We simultaneously recorded from 11,262 ± 2,282 (mean ± s.d.) excitatory neurons, over nine sessions in six mice using 2-photon imaging of GCaMP6s in an 11-plane configuration ( 29 ) ( Fig. 1A,B , Movie S1 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: This is consistent with neuroanatomy: primary sensory cortex receives innervation both from neuromodulatory systems carrying state information, and from higher-order cortices which can encode fine-grained behavioral variables

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: This dimension summarized the mean activity of all cells in the population, and variations along it reflected both spontaneous alternation of up and down phases and differences in mean population response between stimuli.

span.label: reliable variance is defined by double cross-validation: neurons split into two spatially separate sets, timepoints split into train and test, and only variance that covaries across both splits counts
span.quote: We divided the recorded neurons into two spatially segregated sets, and divided the recorded timepoints into two equal halves (training and test; Fig. 1I ). The training timepoints were used to find the dimensions in each cell set’s activity that maximally covary with each other. These dimensions are termed Shared Variance Components (SVCs). Activity in the test time-points was then projected onto each SVC ( Fig. 1J ), and the correlation between projections from the two cell sets ( Fig. 1K ) provided an estimate of the reliable variance in that SVC (see Methods and Appendix ).

span.label: the behavioural regressor is not chosen in advance but discovered, by taking a thousand principal components of facial motion rather than naming which movements should matter
span.quote: We extracted a 1,000-dimensional summary of the motor actions visible on the mouse’s face by applying principal component analysis to the spatial distribution of facial motion at each moment in time ( 36 ).

span.label: the hand-picked arousal variables are shown to be redundant once the video is used, which is how the paper argues the old low-dimensional accounts were glimpses of something larger
span.quote: Moreover, adding these three explicit predictors to the video signal increased the explained variance by less than 1% ( Fig. 2I ), even though the running signal provided information not derived from video.

span.label: the paper states what its own method cannot see, and distinguishes its phenomenon from the fast one by a timescale its sampling rate excludes
span.quote: Indeed, up/down phases could not even have been detected in our recordings, which scanned the cortex every 400 ms.

span.label: the claim of high dimensionality is stress-tested against sample size: reliability of higher components rises with neuron count, so the reported dimensionality is a floor
span.quote: Thousands of neurons were required to reliably characterize activity in hundreds of dimensions, and the estimated reliability of higher SVCs increased with the number of neurons analyzed ( Fig. S7A-E ), suggesting that recordings of larger populations would identify yet more dimensions.

span.label: decoding is used as the check on the subspace geometry - if stimulus information really is confined to one subspace, a classifier reading the others should fail
span.quote: Decoding from the stimulus space yielded a cross-validated error rate of 10.1 ± 4.0 %; activity in the spontaneous- or behavior-only spaces yielded errors of 53.1 ± 6.4 % and 56.8 ± 6.7 %, no better than randomly-chosen dimensions ( Fig. 4F ).

span.label: the imaging result is repeated in a different preparation and a different recording modality, eight probes across forebrain, before the brain-wide claim is made
span.quote: To show this, we used 8 Neuropixels probes ( 37 ) to simultaneously record from frontal, sensorimotor, visual and retrosplenial cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, and midbrain ( Fig. 3A,B ).

span.label: a spatial null is run on the sorted activity continuum: position on it does not track position in the tissue, so the structure is not topographic
span.quote: Position on this continuum bore little relation to actual distances in the imaged tissue ( Fig. S6 ), suggesting that this activity was not organized topographically.

span.label: trial-to-trial variability is decomposed into a multiplicative part inside the stimulus subspace and an additive part outside it, which is what lets a long-running either/or dispute be answered with both
span.quote: Trial-to-trial variability of sensory responses comprised additive ongoing activity in the behavior subspace, and multiplicative modulation in the stimulus subspace, resolving apparently conflicting findings concerning the additive or multiplicative nature of cortical variability ( 39 – 42 ).

span.label: the multiplicative gain is not left as a fitted nuisance parameter but predicted from the behavioural video, tying the statistical model back to an observable
span.quote: Furthermore, the multiplicative gain on each trial could be predicted from facial motion energy ( r = 0.61 ± 0.02 SE, cross-validated), and closely matched activity in the shared subspace ( r = 0.73 ± 0.06 SE, cross-validated; Fig. 4L ).

span.label: the affine model is tested and rejected, so the absence of additive variability within the stimulus subspace is a checked result rather than an assumption
span.quote: Although ongoing activity in the behavior-only subspace and visual responses in the stimulus-only subspace added independently, we did not observe additive variability within the stimulus-only space itself: an “affine” model also including an additive term did not significantly increase explained variance over the multiplicative model ( p > 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

span.label: The dimensionality estimate is bounded by the number of neurons recorded; larger populations would reveal still more dimensions.
span.quote: Thousands of neurons were required to reliably characterize activity in hundreds of dimensions, and the estimated reliability of higher SVCs increased with the number of neurons analyzed ( Fig. S7A-E ), suggesting that recordings of larger populations would identify yet more dimensions.

span.label: The imaging frame rate (400 ms per cortical scan) makes fast up/down phases undetectable in this dataset.
span.quote: Indeed, up/down phases could not even have been detected in our recordings, which scanned the cortex every 400 ms.

span.label: The unexplained dimensions of reliable variance are not identified; they may be motor activity invisible on the face or internal cognitive variables.
span.quote: The remaining dimensions and variance might in part reflect motor activity not visible on the face or only decodable by more advanced methods ( 43 – 48 ), or they might reflect internal cognitive variables such as motivational drives.

span.label: the recording rate makes the fast up/down phenomenon undetectable in the imaging data
span.quote: Indeed, up/down phases could not even have been detected in our recordings, which scanned the cortex every 400 ms.

span.label: most of the reliable variance is still unexplained, and the paper offers two quite different candidates without deciding
span.quote: The remaining dimensions and variance might in part reflect motor activity not visible on the face or only decodable by more advanced methods ( 43 – 48 ), or they might reflect internal cognitive variables such as motivational drives.

span.label: the dimensionality reported is bounded by the number of neurons recorded, not by the brain
span.quote: Thousands of neurons were required to reliably characterize activity in hundreds of dimensions, and the estimated reliability of higher SVCs increased with the number of neurons analyzed ( Fig. S7A-E ), suggesting that recordings of larger populations would identify yet more dimensions.

span.label: the recapitulation account is not excluded, only shown to be unsupported by the similarity statistic on its own
span.quote: While our results do not exclude that genuine recapitulation could occur in other behavioral circumstances, they reinforce the need for careful statistical analysis before drawing this conclusion: even a single dimension of common rate fluctuation is sufficient for some previously-applied statistical methods to report similar population activity ( 49 ).

span.label: a train-test split applied simultaneously along two axes - cells and time - to define which variance counts as signal rather than relying on a noise model
span.quote: We divided the recorded neurons into two spatially segregated sets, and divided the recorded timepoints into two equal halves (training and test; Fig. 1I ). The training timepoints were used to find the dimensions in each cell set’s activity that maximally covary with each other. These dimensions are termed Shared Variance Components (SVCs). Activity in the test time-points was then projected onto each SVC ( Fig. 1J ), and the correlation between projections from the two cell sets ( Fig. 1K ) provided an estimate of the reliable variance in that SVC (see Methods and Appendix ).

span.label: motion energy and its principal components, used to turn a video of a face into a thousand-dimensional behavioural regressor without deciding in advance which movements matter
span.quote: We extracted a 1,000-dimensional summary of the motor actions visible on the mouse’s face by applying principal component analysis to the spatial distribution of facial motion at each moment in time ( 36 ).

span.label: reduced rank regression, used to ask how few behavioural dimensions suffice rather than how much total variance behaviour explains
span.quote: This multidimensional behavior measure predicted approximately twice as much variance as the three arousal variables ( Fig. 2D-J , Movie S3 ).

span.label: cortical variability - as random noise, as recapitulation of prior experience, or as encoding of behaviour; three incompatible readings of one measured quantity, named together by the authors
span.quote: Cortical variability and spontaneous activity have been variously proposed to represent random noise, recall of prior experience, or encoding of ongoing behavioral and cognitive variables.

span.label: variability - independent across cells (harmless to coding) versus correlated (harmful or not, depending on its geometry); the distinction that makes the orthogonality result matter
span.quote: Variability that is independent across cells – such as the Poisson-like variability produced in balanced recurrent networks ( 25 ) – presents little impediment to information coding, as reliable signals can still be extracted as weighted sums over a large enough population.

span.label: correlated variability - mimicking stimulus differences, and so corrupting the code, versus lying orthogonal to them, and so carrying something else
span.quote: If correlated variability mimics differences in responses to different stimuli, it can compromise stimulus encoding ( 26 , 27 ). Conversely, correlated variability in dimensions orthogonal to those encoding stimuli has no adverse impact on coding ( 28 ), and might instead reflect encoding of signals other than visual inputs.

span.label: slow multi-second alternation between two sub-populations versus fast up/down phases modulating all neurons together; the same raster read at two timescales
span.quote: The fast-timescale structure modulated nearly all neurons in the same direction, leading to rapid fluctuations in the total population rate (“up and down phases”); by contrast, the structure seen at lower time scales was dominated by alternation in the activity of different neuronal populations, and steadier total activity

span.label: similarity between spontaneous and evoked activity - as evidence of replayed experience versus as a mean-rate artefact; the paper argues the statistic cannot distinguish them
span.quote: These results therefore demonstrate that the statistical similarity of firing patterns during stimulation and ongoing activity need not imply recapitulation of previous sensory experiences, merely that cortex exhibits mean rate fluctuations with or without sensory inputs.

span.label: arousal as three hand-picked variables versus behaviour as a thousand videographic dimensions; the first turns out to be a projection of the second
span.quote: Moreover, adding these three explicit predictors to the video signal increased the explained variance by less than 1% ( Fig. 2I ), even though the running signal provided information not derived from video.

span.label: reliable variance - defined operationally as what survives a split across both cells and time, not as what exceeds a noise threshold
span.quote: We divided the recorded neurons into two spatially segregated sets, and divided the recorded timepoints into two equal halves (training and test; Fig. 1I ). The training timepoints were used to find the dimensions in each cell set’s activity that maximally covary with each other. These dimensions are termed Shared Variance Components (SVCs). Activity in the test time-points was then projected onto each SVC ( Fig. 1J ), and the correlation between projections from the two cell sets ( Fig. 1K ) provided an estimate of the reliable variance in that SVC (see Methods and Appendix ).

span.label: extends → Previous reports of low-dimensional locomotion and arousal correlates in visual cortex (refs 8, 10-16, 33)
span.quote: Our data are consistent with previous reports describing low-dimensional correlates of locomotion and arousal in visual cortex ( 8 , 10 – 16 , 33 ), but suggest these results were glimpses of a much larger set of non-visual variables encoded by ongoing activity patterns.

span.label: contradicts → Studies reporting similarity between spontaneous activity and sensory responses as evidence for recapitulation of sensory experience (refs 2-7)
span.quote: We also observed a similarity, but found it arose nearly exclusively from one dimension of neural activity.

span.label: extends → Conflicting prior findings on whether cortical variability is additive or multiplicative (refs 39-42)
span.quote: Trial-to-trial variability of sensory responses comprised additive ongoing activity in the behavior subspace, and multiplicative modulation in the stimulus subspace, resolving apparently conflicting findings concerning the additive or multiplicative nature of cortical variability ( 39 – 42 ).

span.label: critiques → studies inferring recapitulation of sensory experience from statistical similarity between spontaneous and evoked activity
span.quote: While our results do not exclude that genuine recapitulation could occur in other behavioral circumstances, they reinforce the need for careful statistical analysis before drawing this conclusion: even a single dimension of common rate fluctuation is sufficient for some previously-applied statistical methods to report similar population activity ( 49 ).

span.label: extends → reports of low-dimensional locomotion and arousal correlates in visual cortex, which the paper recasts as glimpses of a much larger set
span.quote: Our data are consistent with previous reports describing low-dimensional correlates of locomotion and arousal in visual cortex ( 8 , 10 – 16 , 33 ), but suggest these results were glimpses of a much larger set of non-visual variables encoded by ongoing activity patterns.

span.label: supports → the resolution of the additive-versus-multiplicative dispute about cortical variability, by assigning each to a different subspace
span.quote: Trial-to-trial variability of sensory responses comprised additive ongoing activity in the behavior subspace, and multiplicative modulation in the stimulus subspace, resolving apparently conflicting findings concerning the additive or multiplicative nature of cortical variability ( 39 – 42 ).

span.label: contradicts → the view that trial-to-trial variability in sensory cortex is primarily unstructured noise
span.quote: Thus, visual cortical population activity, despite its apparently noisy structure, reliably encodes an orthogonal fusion of sensory and multidimensional behavioral information.

span.label: builds-on → the anatomical fact that primary sensory cortex receives both neuromodulatory state input and higher-order cortical input
span.quote: This is consistent with neuroanatomy: primary sensory cortex receives innervation both from neuromodulatory systems carrying state information, and from higher-order cortices which can encode fine-grained behavioral variables ( 9 ).

span.label: spontaneous activity —distinct-from→ random noise
span.quote: Thus, visual cortical population activity, despite its apparently noisy structure, reliably encodes an orthogonal fusion of sensory and multidimensional behavioral information.

span.label: spontaneous activity —distinct-from→ recapitulation
span.quote: These results therefore demonstrate that the statistical similarity of firing patterns during stimulation and ongoing activity need not imply recapitulation of previous sensory experiences, merely that cortex exhibits mean rate fluctuations with or without sensory inputs.

span.label: reliable variance —operationalised-as→ Shared Variance Component Analysis
span.quote: We divided the recorded neurons into two spatially segregated sets, and divided the recorded timepoints into two equal halves (training and test; Fig. 1I ). The training timepoints were used to find the dimensions in each cell set’s activity that maximally covary with each other. These dimensions are termed Shared Variance Components (SVCs). Activity in the test time-points was then projected onto each SVC ( Fig. 1J ), and the correlation between projections from the two cell sets ( Fig. 1K ) provided an estimate of the reliable variance in that SVC (see Methods and Appendix ).

span.label: arousal —part-of→ facial motion
span.quote: Moreover, adding these three explicit predictors to the video signal increased the explained variance by less than 1% ( Fig. 2I ), even though the running signal provided information not derived from video.

span.label: stimulus-only subspace —distinct-from→ behavior-only subspace
span.quote: Thus, overlap in the spaces encoding sensory and behavioral variables arises primarily because both can change the mean firing rate of the population: the precise patterns of increases and decreases about this change in mean were essentially orthogonal ( Fig. 4E ).

span.label: shared subspace —same-as→ up and down phases
span.quote: This dimension summarized the mean activity of all cells in the population, and variations along it reflected both spontaneous alternation of up and down phases and differences in mean population response between stimuli.

span.label: facial motion —causes→ multiplicative gain
span.quote: Furthermore, the multiplicative gain on each trial could be predicted from facial motion energy ( r = 0.61 ± 0.02 SE, cross-validated), and closely matched activity in the shared subspace ( r = 0.73 ± 0.06 SE, cross-validated; Fig. 4L ).

span.label: up and down phases —distinct-from→ spontaneous activity
span.quote: The slowness of these fluctuations suggests a different underlying phenomenon to previously-studied up and down phases ( 5 , 31 – 34 ), which alternate at a much faster timescale (~100 ms instead of multiple seconds) and correlate with most neurons positively.

span.label: arousal —operationalised-as→ locomotion
span.quote: Fluctuations in the first principal component (PC) occurred over a timescale of many seconds ( Fig. S3 ), and were coupled to running, whisking, and pupil diameter.

span.label: Shared Variance Components —operationalised-as→ reliable variance
span.quote: The fraction of reliable variance in the first SVC was 97% ( Fig. 1K,L ), implying that only 3% of the variance along this dimension reflected independent noise.

span.label: thalamus —part-of→ forebrain
span.quote: To show this, we used 8 Neuropixels probes ( 37 ) to simultaneously record from frontal, sensorimotor, visual and retrosplenial cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, and midbrain ( Fig. 3A,B ).

span.label: statistics

The training timepoints were used to find the dimensions in each cell set’s activity that maximally covary with each other. These dimensions are termed Shared Variance Components (SVCs). Activity in the test time-points was then projected onto each SVC ( Fig. 1J ), and the correlation between projections from the two cell sets ( Fig. 1K ) provided an estimate of the reliable variance in that SVC (see Methods and Appendix ).

span.label: statistics
span.quote: This multidimensional behavior measure predicted approximately twice as much variance as the three arousal variables ( Fig. 2D-J , Movie S3 ).

span.label: statistics
span.quote: The magnitude of reliable spontaneous variance was distributed across dimensions according to a power law of exponent 1.14 ( Fig. 1M ). This value is larger than the power law exponents close to 1.0 seen for stimulus responses ( 35 ), but still indicates a high-dimensional signal.

span.label: statistics
span.quote: All brain areas contained a sampling of neurons from the entire continuum ( Fig. 3E , right), suggesting that a multidimensional structure of ongoing activity is distributed throughout the brain.

span.label: statistics
span.quote: Although ongoing activity in the behavior-only subspace and visual responses in the stimulus-only subspace added independently, we did not observe additive variability within the stimulus-only space itself: an “affine” model also including an additive term did not significantly increase explained variance over the multiplicative model ( p > 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

span.label: statistics
span.quote: Furthermore, the multiplicative gain on each trial could be predicted from facial motion energy ( r = 0.61 ± 0.02 SE, cross-validated), and closely matched activity in the shared subspace ( r = 0.73 ± 0.06 SE, cross-validated; Fig. 4L ).

span.label: Ongoing (spontaneous) population activity in mouse visual cortex reliably encodes a latent signal spanning at least 100 linear dimensions rather than one or two noise-like factors.
span.quote: Ongoing population activity in visual cortex reliably encoded a latent signal of at least 100 linear dimensions, and possibly many more.

span.label: The single largest dimension of ongoing activity tracks arousal and drives roughly half the neurons up while driving the other half down, so it is not a global rate increase.
span.quote: The largest dimension correlated with arousal and modulated about half of the neurons positively and half negatively.

span.label: A high-dimensional description of facial movement predicts about twice as much neural variance as the three standard arousal measures (running, pupil diameter and whisking) combined.
span.quote: This multidimensional behavior measure predicted approximately twice as much variance as the three arousal variables

span.label: The same multidimensional behaviour-related activity structure is not confined to visual cortex but is present in neurons sampled across the forebrain.
span.quote: suggesting that a multidimensional structure of ongoing activity is distributed throughout the brain

span.label: The neural subspaces encoding visual stimuli and encoding behaviour share only a single dimension, which is the population mean firing rate; all the finer patterns of increase and decrease are orthogonal between the two.
span.quote: Thus, overlap in the spaces encoding sensory and behavioral variables arises primarily because both can change the mean firing rate of the population: the precise patterns of increases and decreases about this change in mean were essentially orthogonal

span.label: Stimulus identity can be decoded accurately from the stimulus-only subspace but not at all from the behaviour-only or spontaneous-only subspaces, which perform no better than random dimensions.
span.quote: Decoding from the stimulus space yielded a cross-validated error rate of 10.1 ± 4.0 %; activity in the spontaneous- or behavior-only spaces yielded errors of 53.1 ± 6.4 % and 56.8 ± 6.7 %, no better than randomly-chosen dimensions

span.label: Trial-to-trial response variability decomposes into multiplicative gain modulation inside the stimulus subspace plus additive ongoing activity in dimensions orthogonal to it.
span.quote: Trial-to-trial variability in population responses to repeated stimulus presentations reflected a combination of multiplicative modulation in the stimulus-space, and additive modulation in orthogonal dimensions.

span.label: Thalamic neurons are the most strongly behaviour-modulated population recorded, with 35.7% of their total variance predictable from facial video.
span.quote: with neurons in thalamus predicted best (35.7% of total variance, 59% of estimated maximum)

span.label: 97% of the variance in the first shared component was reliable, leaving 3% for independent noise
span.quote: The fraction of reliable variance in the first SVC was 97% ( Fig. 1K,L ), implying that only 3% of the variance along this dimension reflected independent noise.

span.label: reliable spontaneous variance decayed across dimensions as a power law of exponent 1.14, steeper than for stimulus responses but still high-dimensional
span.quote: The magnitude of reliable spontaneous variance was distributed across dimensions according to a power law of exponent 1.14 ( Fig. 1M ). This value is larger than the power law exponents close to 1.0 seen for stimulus responses ( 35 ), but still indicates a high-dimensional signal.

span.label: the three explicit arousal variables together explained about half the variance of the first neural principal component
span.quote: These arousal-related variables correlated with each other ( Fig. S4A,B ), and together accounted for approximately 50% of the variance of the first neural PC ( Fig. 1E , Fig. S4C ).

span.label: about 57% of neurons correlated positively with the first PC and the rest negatively, so two sub-populations alternate
span.quote: Correlation with the first PC was positive or negative in approximately similar numbers of neurons (57% ± 6.7% SE positive), indicating that two large sub-populations of neurons alternate their activity ( Fig. 1F,G ).

span.label: multidimensional facial behaviour predicted roughly twice the variance the three arousal variables did
span.quote: This multidimensional behavior measure predicted approximately twice as much variance as the three arousal variables ( Fig. 2D-J , Movie S3 ).

span.label: prediction kept improving up to at least 16 behavioural dimensions, so visual cortex encodes at least that many motor dimensions
span.quote: Prediction quality continued to increase with up to 16 dimensions of video-graphic information (and beyond, in some recordings), suggesting that visual cortex encodes at least 16 dimensions of motor information.

span.label: those dimensions captured 21% of total population variance against 11% for the three-variable model
span.quote: These dimensions together accounted for 21%± 1% SE of the total population variance (31% ± 3% of the reliable variance; Fig. 2H ), substantially more than the three-dimensional model of neural activity using running, pupil area and whisking (11% ± 1% SE of the total variance, 17% ± 1% SE of the reliable variance).

span.label: adding running, pupil and whisking to the video improved prediction by less than 1%, even though running is not visible in the face video
span.quote: Moreover, adding these three explicit predictors to the video signal increased the explained variance by less than 1% ( Fig. 2I ), even though the running signal provided information not derived from video.

span.label: every recorded brain area contained neurons across the whole activity continuum, so the structure is distributed rather than localised
span.quote: All brain areas contained a sampling of neurons from the entire continuum ( Fig. 3E , right), suggesting that a multidimensional structure of ongoing activity is distributed throughout the brain.

span.label: thalamic neurons were the best predicted by behaviour, at 35.7% of total variance
span.quote: The amount of behavioral modulation differed between brain regions, with neurons in thalamus predicted best (35.7% of total variance, 59% of estimated maximum).

span.label: behavioural prediction was best at zero lag and decayed over seconds, full width at half maximum 2.5 s
span.quote: The timescale of videographic prediction was again broad: neural activity was best predicted from instantaneous behavior, decaying slowly over time lags of multiple seconds ( Figs. 3G-H , S10 ), with a full-width at half-max of 2.5±0.4 s (mean ± SE).

span.label: stimulus and behaviour subspaces overlapped in essentially one dimension, which is the population mean rate
span.quote: Thus, overlap in the spaces encoding sensory and behavioral variables arises primarily because both can change the mean firing rate of the population: the precise patterns of increases and decreases about this change in mean were essentially orthogonal ( Fig. 4E ).

span.label: a classifier decoded stimuli at 10% error from the stimulus subspace and at chance from the behaviour or spontaneous subspaces
span.quote: Decoding from the stimulus space yielded a cross-validated error rate of 10.1 ± 4.0 %; activity in the spontaneous- or behavior-only spaces yielded errors of 53.1 ± 6.4 % and 56.8 ± 6.7 %, no better than randomly-chosen dimensions ( Fig. 4F ).

span.label: the behaviour subspace was active before the stimulus and continued unchanged through it, while the stimulus subspace was silent then active
span.quote: During gray-screen periods there was no activity in the stimulus-only subspace, but when the stimuli appeared this subspace became very active. By contrast, activity in the behavioronly subspace was present prior to stimulus presentation, and continued unchanged when the stimulus appeared.

span.label: a purely multiplicative trial-varying gain accounted for 89% of the variance in the stimulus subspace
span.quote: A model in which stimulus responses are multiplied by a trial-dependent factor accurately captured the data, accounting for 89% ± 0.1% SE of the variance in the stimulus subspace ( Fig. 4K ).

span.label: that gain was predictable from facial motion at r = 0.61 cross-validated
span.quote: Furthermore, the multiplicative gain on each trial could be predicted from facial motion energy ( r = 0.61 ± 0.02 SE, cross-validated), and closely matched activity in the shared subspace ( r = 0.73 ± 0.06 SE, cross-validated; Fig. 4L ).

span.label: adding an additive term to the multiplicative model did not significantly improve it
span.quote: Although ongoing activity in the behavior-only subspace and visual responses in the stimulus-only subspace added independently, we did not observe additive variability within the stimulus-only space itself: an “affine” model also including an additive term did not significantly increase explained variance over the multiplicative model ( p > 0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

span.label: stimulus and behaviour representations were mixed in the same neurons rather than carried by separate populations
span.quote: There were not separate sets of neurons encoding stimuli and behavioral variables; instead, representations of sensory and behavioral information were mixed together in the same cell population.

span.label: recordings in darkness and with a gray screen did not differ
span.quote: Six of nine recordings were performed in darkness, but we did not observe differences between these recordings (shown in red on all plots) and recordings with gray screen (yellow on all plots).

span.label: position on the sorted activity continuum bore little relation to position in the tissue
span.quote: Position on this continuum bore little relation to actual distances in the imaged tissue ( Fig. S6 ), suggesting that this activity was not organized topographically.
